summary: Specifies the RPKI Repository Delta Protocol, which relying parties use to fetch published RPKI data over HTTPS. It uses an update notification file that lists a snapshot and deltas, and is designed to scale with caches and CDNs. Later RFCs update it.

eli5.summary: Instead of reading the whole phone book again each day, you just fetch a list of what changed.

questions: what is an rpki update notification file
how often can rrdp be polled
subtitle: How RPKI repositories hand out their data over HTTPS using a snapshot, a list of changes and a small notification file.

tldr.problem: RPKI repositories were only reachable through rsync, which costs the server significant CPU and memory for every connection and is weak against denial-of-service when thousands of Relying Parties query a few central repositories.
tldr.mechanism: The repository publishes an Update Notification File that points to the current Snapshot File and to Delta Files for recent serial numbers. Relying Parties fetch these immutable files over HTTPS, so they can be cached or served by a CDN.
tldr.outcome: RRDP is an additional distribution mechanism that can coexist with rsync. It was proposed as a possible future replacement, but that transition is explicitly out of scope. Later RFCs update it.

today: RFC 8182 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9674 and RFC 9697; it has not been obsoleted. Read it together with those updates.

sections.title: Why rsync Was Not Enough
sections.content:
In the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), Certificate Authorities publish certificates, signed objects, manifests and CRLs to repositories, and Relying Parties copy them down to validate them. Until this RFC the access method was rsync.

The RFC names two problems. First, rsync is built to limit the data transferred, but the server pays significant CPU and memory for every connection. With thousands of Relying Parties querying a small number of central repositories, that makes the repositories weak to denial-of-service attacks. Second, there are no well-supported rsync server and client libraries, so implementations must call an rsync binary, which is inefficient and fragile and makes errors hard to report.

RRDP is the alternative: files fetched over HTTPS that the server can compute once for all clients and that caches can serve.
sections.eli5: Asking a librarian to hand-pick pages for each visitor is slow when thousands of people show up. It is much easier to put ready-made copies on a table and let everyone take one.

sections.title: The Three Kinds of File
sections.content:
A certificate whose Repository Server supports RRDP carries a Subject Information Access (SIA) pointer to an Update Notification File. That small file holds a session_id (a version 4 UUID), a serial number, a link to the latest complete Snapshot File, and links to Delta Files for each revision from a point the server chooses up to the current one.

A Relying Party that sees a location for the first time downloads the notification, then the snapshot, and records the location, the session_id and the serial. Later it re-fetches the notification, at most once per minute. If a contiguous chain of deltas leads from its serial to the current one, it applies them. If the chain has a gap, or the session_id changed, it does a full resynchronization from the snapshot.

Snapshots and deltas for a given session_id and serial are an immutable record, so they can be cached indefinitely. The notification file is polled for changes, so it may not be cached for longer than one minute.
sections.eli5: There is a tiny note that says what version the collection is on, a full copy of everything, and a stack of small change slips. You read the note first, and then pick the slips or the full copy.

sections.title: What the Repository Server Does
sections.content:
On initialization the server MUST generate a new random version 4 UUID as the session_id, and generate a Snapshot File for serial number ONE holding every object it is responsible for (possibly zero publish elements). It then publishes an Update Notification File with that session_id, serial ONE, one snapshot reference and no deltas.

When it receives updates from a Certificate Authority it MUST generate new snapshot and Delta Files within one minute. It MAY combine updates from several CAs but never delay any CA's publication by more than one minute. The new serial MUST be exactly one greater than the current one. The new Delta File holds all new, replaced and withdrawn objects as a single change set, and the new Snapshot File holds all current objects. Each file is placed at a URL unique to the session_id and serial.

Older Delta Files that, combined with all newer ones, would exceed the size of the snapshot MUST be left out of the new notification, so Relying Parties never download more than necessary. If the server cannot do all this it MUST perform a full re-initialization.
sections.eli5: Each time something changes, the server writes a new change slip and a fresh full copy, and bumps the version number by exactly one. If it ever loses track, it starts over with a new collection name.

sections.title: What the Relying Party Does
sections.content:
A Relying Party that finds a valid certificate with an RRDP SIA entry SHOULD use the protocol. It MUST download the Update Notification File, check its format and reject it if verification fails, and compare the session_id to the last one known for that file's location. The session_id alone MUST NOT identify a session, because a malicious server can reuse another server's session_id.

If the session_id matches and a contiguous delta chain exists, the Relying Party MAY fetch the deltas, and must process them in serial order. Each delta must match the hash in the notification, carry the notification's session_id, and have a serial exactly one greater than the last processed. When a delta withdraws or replaces an object, the Relying Party MUST check that the object came from the same Repository Server, or a malicious server could make it delete or change arbitrary objects.

If any delta is rejected, or the session_id changed, the Relying Party MUST process the Snapshot File instead, after checking its hash, its session_id and that its serial is greater than the last processed. If the snapshot is rejected, RRDP cannot be used for that server.

Polling: a Relying Party MUST NOT poll more often than once every 1 minute and MUST use the If-Modified-Since header. It is advised to keep old objects in its cache and to retry, and may fall back to other access methods listed in the certificate's SIA.
sections.eli5: You check the note, make sure it is from the right place, and then apply the change slips in order. If any slip looks wrong or you missed some, you throw them out and use the full copy.

sections.title: The XML File Formats
sections.content:
All three files are XML in the namespace http://www.ripe.net/rpki/rrdp, encoded as US-ASCII, with version equal to 1, and are described by a RELAX NG schema in the RFC. A Relying Party MUST reject a file that is not well-formed or does not match the schema.

  • Notification (notification): attributes session_id and serial; exactly one snapshot element and zero or more delta elements, each with a uri and a SHA-256 hash (hex) of the referenced file. Deltas must form a contiguous run of serials up to the current serial, and need not be ordered.
  • Snapshot (snapshot): one publish element per current object, with its rsync uri and the object's content in base64. Its session_id and serial MUST match the notification's reference.
  • Delta (delta): the changes for exactly one serial increment, as publish elements (with a hash of the replaced object when one is replaced) and withdraw elements (with the hash of the withdrawn object).

The tag attribute from the publication protocol in RFC 8181 is not used here. The schema comments liken the snapshot to DNS AXFR and the delta to DNS IXFR. It is RECOMMENDED that CAs send all changes for one key pair, including the new manifest and CRL, as one atomic update.
sections.eli5: The note, the full copy and the change slips are all written in the same tidy, labeled format, so a computer can check them quickly for mistakes before using them.

sections.title: Caching, Coexistence and HTTPS
sections.content:
Snapshot and Delta Files never change after they are published, which lets a single HTTP server or a CDN distribute them. The RFC recommends cache lifetimes in the order of hours or days for them to save cache space, and says servers SHOULD keep old snapshots, and deltas that are no longer listed, for at least 5 minutes so a Relying Party that fetched the notification just before an update does not hit a missing file. The notification file should not be cached for longer than 1 minute, with an exception: serving a stale notification is better than serving none. A server may suggest a poll interval, but longer than 1 hour is NOT RECOMMENDED. Servers should avoid producing new serials much more often than once per minute, since bursts of manifest and CRL refreshes can be combined.

Each object is listed with both its content hash and its rsync URI, so the same repository can be served over rsync and RRDP, and tools can combine objects from repositories of different types.

On HTTPS, a man in the middle cannot forge validly signed RPKI data but can withhold or replay it. Relying Parties SHOULD validate the TLS certificate and host name, and log problems, but MUST keep retrieving the data even on errors, because the signed data is validated anyway and such failures are often configuration mistakes.
sections.eli5: Because the change slips never get edited, anyone can keep photocopies and hand them out. Only the version note must be fresh, so it is only kept for a minute at most.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RRDP only moves RPKI objects from a Repository Server to a Relying Party. Certificates, CRLs and CMS-wrapped objects are already protected by object security, including signed manifests, so they can be validated even though the Repository Server is not trusted. The RFC makes no change to RPKI validation procedures.

HTTPS, unlike rsync, offers a channel security mechanism and makes some denial-of-service attacks harder, though the RFC calls it not a cure-all. Supporting both RRDP and rsync gives a malicious CA more URIs to send a Relying Party after, but a CA could already supply an effectively infinite series of URIs; the only real answer is for the Relying Party to bound the work it will do.

Because a delta is a unit, a Relying Party may not be able to start processing it until it is fully received. The RFC says RRDP behaves closer to a transactional system, which probably leads to higher reliability. IANA updated the reference for id-ad-rpkiNotify to point to this document.
sections.eli5: Every item has its own tamper-proof seal, so even if the delivery truck is not trusted, a bad package gets spotted when you open it.

sections.title: Place in the RPKI Ecosystem
sections.content: RRDP is described as an additional repository distribution mechanism. The introduction says that in time it may replace rsync as the only mandatory-to-implement mechanism, but that transition is outside the scope of the document. It is consistent in data structures with the publication protocol in RFC 8181.
sections.eli5: The new way sits next to the old way, and maybe one day it will be the only one everyone must support.

data.title: Update Notification File
data.code:
<notification xmlns="http://www.ripe.net/rpki/rrdp"
      version="1"
      session_id="9df4b597-af9e-4dca-bdda-719cce2c4e28"
      serial="3">
  <snapshot uri="https://host/9d-8/3/snapshot.xml" hash="AB"/>
  <delta serial="3" uri="https://host/9d-8/3/delta.xml" hash="CD"/>
  <delta serial="2" uri="https://host/9d-8/2/delta.xml" hash="EF"/>
</notification>
